🚀 We’re Hiring | Generative AI Engineer
Are you passionate about building production-grade Generative AI systems and working with cutting-edge technologies such as RAG, Agentic AI, LLMs, Multimodal AI, and Cloud AI platforms?
Cyrino is looking for a Generative AI Engineer to design, build, and deploy robust AI solutions across Azure and AWS.
🔹 What You’ll Work On
Build end-to-end RAG pipelines with chunking, embeddings, hybrid retrieval, and re-ranking
Develop Multi-Agent / Agentic AI systems using LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Semantic Kernel
Build LLM-based structured document extraction for PDFs, forms, and contracts
Implement AI compliance guardrails, content filtering, and output validation
Develop conversational AI and chatbot backends using Python, FastAPI & REST APIs
Explore Multimodal AI using vision + text for document understanding and content generation
Implement AI evaluation & observability using LangSmith, Ragas, and custom tracing
Build MLOps / CI-CD pipelines and deploy AI workloads using Docker & Kubernetes
Work directly with clients and stakeholders to understand requirements and present solution designs
Mentor junior engineers through code reviews and technical discussions
🛠️ Key Skills
AI / GenAI: RAG, Agentic AI, Multi-Agent Systems, LLM Fine-tuning, Prompt Engineering
Frameworks: LangChain, LlamaIndex, Semantic Kernel, PyTorch, TensorFlow, Scikit-learn
Vector Databases: OpenSearch, Pinecone
Development: Python, FastAPI, REST APIs
Cloud: Azure OpenAI, Azure AI Search, Databricks, AWS Bedrock, SageMaker, OpenSearch
MLOps: CI/CD, Docker, Kubernetes
Evaluation: LangSmith, Ragas, AI tracing & observability
🎯 What We’re Looking For
3–5 years of hands-on software engineering experience
At least 2 years focused on AI/ML or GenAI development
Proven experience delivering at least one production RAG or Agentic AI system
Strong Python engineering skills
Understanding of transformers, embedding models, and LLM inference
Production experience with Azure or AWS AI services
Strong communication skills with technical and non-technical stakeholders
Bachelor's/Master's degree in Computer Science, Engineering, or equivalent practical experience
⭐ Nice to Have: Knowledge Graphs, Neo4j, AWS Neptune, graph-augmented RAG, multimodal models, Delta Lake, Spark, event-driven ingestion, or open-source AI/ML contributions.

През 2023 година отидох на важна среща с потенциален клиент в Лондон.
 
Влязох в конферентната зала на компания с 200 души в централен Лондон.
 
Мъж на около 55 години стана да ме посрещне с ръкостискане.
 
Той се усмихна учтиво и каза - „Здравейте, къде е шефът ви днес?"
 
Останах онемяла точно 3 секунди преди да отговоря спокойно.
 
„Аз съм шефът. Аз съм собственикът на recruitment агенцията, за която говорим."
 
Лицето му се промени за части от секундата - от усмивка към неудобство. ☝️
 
Той се опита да оправи ситуацията с шеговити коментари за кафе.
 
Проведох срещата професионално, без да покажа гнева или разочарованието си.
 
Подписахме recruitment договор за 10 позиции през следващите 12 месеца. Тогава още нямаха офис в България. Наех им 7 product and software engineers, които влияят позитивно на бизнеса им и до ден днешен.
 
Днес, 3 години по-късно, същият този клиент е един от най-лоялните ми партньори.
 
Ето какво научих от този опит за жените-собственици на бизнеси.
 
Момент на подценяване не определя това, което правите след него.
 
Реакцията ви в тези моменти строи или разрушава дългосрочните отношения.
 
Гневът е валидна емоция, която не трябва да ръководи бизнес решенията ви.
 
Всяка жена-собственик на бизнес има поне 5 такива истории в кариерата си.
 
📌 Как ги трансформираме в стратегическо предимство е реалният въпрос за всяка от нас.
 
Каква е вашата история от момент, в който ви подцениха - искам да чуя в коментарите
 

Три години по-късно най-силният ми отговор на въпроса „Къде е шефът?“ вече не е титлата ми, а хората, екипите и бизнесите, които продължаваме да изграждаме с моя международен team.

Our self-delivery model puts us in a unique position to do this. We hire, train and develop our own people and manage the end-to-end processes behind how work is planned and delivered. This allows us to continuously improve productivity based on global benchmarks and operational best practices - while delivering carefully curated service experiences across our customers’ sites.
 
Over the past couple of years, we have significantly strengthened our processes - but we can go further. And this is where AI and technology can help.
 
We are already using AI across ISS, from reducing food waste to managing contract scope and water quality. And we are investing in new solutions where we see the greatest potential.
 
One example is workforce planning. Every day, our 10,000 First-line Managers make around 150,000 decisions on overtime, extra hours, re-planning and more. We are currently developing an AI agent to turn large and complex data sets into real-time insights, helping our managers make the best and most cost-effective decisions.
 
We are also looking at the potential of robotics. Around 850 ‘co-bots’ already support our people with selected tasks, such as cleaning large surfaces in airports and hospitals.
 
And through a new programme, we are investigating how ‘humanoid’ robots could further increase productivity in cleaning. We do not yet know how big the potential will be. But if the technology works, our operational expertise puts us in a strong position to turn it into a competitive advantage - complementing the great work our people do every day.
 
When we become more effective and productive, we become more competitive and win more business. And that means hiring more people.
 
I am excited about the potential of Workforce Management powered by technology - and have no doubt it will play a key role in accelerating ISS’ profitable growth.

I looked past the Oracle layoff headline this week into what actually happens to the people who lost their jobs, and the answer is not simple relief.

Oracle's global headcount dropped by about 21,000 in the year ending May 31, a 13 percent cut, even as the company spent 28.5 billion dollars on capex in a single quarter this fiscal year, more than three times what it spent in the same quarter last year. It also signed over 30 billion dollars in new AI cloud contracts in that period. The company is not short on cash. It is short on the specific skills it wants to pay for.

Naukri's own JobSpeak data for August shows India's GCCs growing hiring 10 percent year on year, but AI and ML hiring inside that number grew 31 percent, and hiring for professionals with 8 to 12 years of experience in AI and ML jumped 39 percent. For the 13 to 16 year bracket it jumped 87 percent.

Read those two numbers together and the story changes. A senior Oracle engineer with a decade of cloud or data experience walks into a market that is actively hunting for exactly that profile right now. A senior Oracle engineer whose last five years were legacy application support or routine maintenance walks into the same market and finds almost nothing built for them.

This is the part every layoff headline skips. The job market is not shrinking for experienced people. It is getting sharply more selective about which decade of experience it will pay for. Every laid off professional right now is really being asked one blunt question by the market, whether their last few years were spent building something the AI hiring wave wants, or maintaining something it has already decided to automate around.

What should an AI agent actually be allowed to decide?
This is one of the first questions I'd ask before deploying an agent inside a business.
Giving an agent access to your tools is easy.

Deciding what it can do without asking you is harder.
I use a simple framework:

LOW RISK → Let the agent decide
If the cost of being wrong is small, give it autonomy.
Examples:
→ Categorising support tickets
→ Updating CRM fields
→ Sending routine reminders
→ Summarising meetings
→ Moving tasks between stages
→ Finding and organising information
The agent can act.
No approval needed.

MEDIUM RISK → Agent recommends, human approves
The decision has consequences, but it's still reviewable.
Examples:
→ Choosing which leads deserve immediate attention
→ Drafting a customer response
→ Recommending a discount
→ Prioritising sales opportunities
→ Creating a project plan
→ Flagging an unusual customer issue
The agent does the analysis.
A human makes the final call.

HIGH RISK → Human decides
If the decision can materially affect money, reputation, customers or the business, keep a human in the loop.
Examples:
→ Approving large refunds
→ Signing contracts
→ Hiring or firing
→ Changing pricing strategy
→ Making financial commitments
→ Deleting critical data
→ Sending sensitive information
The agent can prepare the work.
It shouldn't own the decision.

That's the mistake I see businesses making with AI agents.
They ask:
"Can the agent do this?"
The better question is:
"What happens if the agent gets this wrong?"

That answer should determine how much autonomy you give it.
Build the agent around the risk.
Not around what the technology happens to be capable of.

Vibe coding: the freedom recruiters wanted, and the risk nobody planned for

A recruiter can now build a candidate screening tool in an afternoon.
No IT ticket. No vendor contract. No six-month wait.
Just a problem, a prompt and a working prototype.

That's a real shift. For years, recruiters depended on IT teams, software vendors and developers to turn workflow problems into technology solutions. Now they can:
1️⃣ Experiment faster
2️⃣ Own their workflows
3️⃣ Prototype ideas that never would have justified a big technology project
But there's another side.

What happens when that tool touches candidate data?
Salary details. Interview notes. Assessment results. Personal information.
Picture a recruiter pasting CVs and salary expectations into a free AI tool to save time.
Or a home-built screening tool that quietly filters out certain candidates, and nobody notices.

This is no longer just an IT problem. In many regions, hiring data and AI-assisted decisions fall under regulations like GDPR and Singapore's PDPA. Shadow AI in recruitment is a compliance risk, not just a technical one.
So should recruiters stop experimenting?
No. I think the answer is guardrails, not bans.

Here's what I'd put in place:
1️⃣ Use dummy data for prototypes, never real candidate data
2️⃣ No AI tool makes or ranks hiring decisions without human review
3️⃣ Keep a simple register of internal tools, so nothing is invisible
4️⃣ Set a clear trigger for when a prototype goes to security or legal review
5️⃣ Test the output before trusting it, especially for bias
6️⃣ Move successful prototypes into proper governance before scaling

AI gives recruiters more technological freedom.
With that freedom comes responsibility.

The future may not belong to the organisations that experiment the most, but to those that know how to experiment safely.

What's the one guardrail you'd insist on?

Most portfolio ML projects only show you the model that worked. Here's one that also shows you what didn't.

While building WellPulse, a project that predicts a student wellbeing score (1–10) from social-media and behavioral survey data. I found that one feature in the dataset explained 89% of the target's variance completely on its own. A near-tautological shortcut, not a real signal. I excluded it and documented why, instead of quietly using it to inflate my metrics.

Later, hyperparameter tuning genuinely failed to beat the untuned baseline model. I reported that too, instead of re-running it until it "worked."

That's the standard I held the entire build to, end to end, across 13 phases:

→ Data validation via a schema contract that fails loudly on bad data instead of silently
→ EDA and the leakage check above, run before any model ever saw the data
→ 9 model families compared, including LightGBM and XGBoost, against an untuned baseline
→ SHAP explainability, MLflow experiment tracking, and a model registry
→ A FastAPI backend with real per-user auth, Postgres persistence, and check-in history
→ Multi-stage Docker build and GitHub Actions CI/CD
→ Live deployment
→ A weekly automated job that watches live production data for drift

71 tests passing end to end. And the README states the model's real limitations plainly including where its recall is weakest because a project like this is only useful to a hiring manager if it's honest about what a model actually does and doesn't do.

Last week I spoke to 60+ Microsoft AI candidates across ANZ.

Not InMails. Actual calls. Copilot Studio, Azure AI Foundry, Power Platform automation.

Here is what the market actually looks like right now.

Of 60+ conversations, maybe 10 to 12 have genuine production experience. Live deployments, real users, survived a security review. The rest have a POC that impressed a steering group & has not been touched since.

One has run live AI across four hospitals for three years & just signed a 12 month contract at a major Melbourne hospital. $1,000 a day.

One team switched from Copilot to Claude mid project because the output quality was better. Their words.

One developer found a prompt injection hidden in white text on a white background inside a client document. The client had no idea.

One CEO nearly moved his whole organisation to AWS because he tested the free web version of Copilot & it did not read his SharePoint. One demo changed his mind.

Roughly 60% of what clients think needs an agent does not. The misdiagnosis happens before the brief reaches anyone technical.

& the strong people are not on job boards. They are mid contract, running workshops or building internally.

To hiring managers: you cannot see any of this on a CV. Ask every candidate what broke in production & how they fixed it. Specific answer with a timeline, good sign. Pivot back to the POC, not ready.

To candidates: the market rewards honesty right now because everyone else is inflating. Know your level & say it.

Worth a chat if you are hiring in this space. No pitch.

The AI conversation in 2026 is shifting from "can it code?" to "can it audit itself?" The most under-discussed development I am tracking is not a new model or a faster inference engine. It is the quiet emergence of "self-validating AI pipelines" that enforce runtime contracts on their own outputs.

I have been auditing teams that deploy AI agents with built-in confidence thresholds and fallback mechanisms. The obvious story is that these systems refuse to act when their certainty drops below a predefined level. The non-obvious lesson is what happens to your operational risk when the AI can detect its own hallucination rate in real time and escalate to a human before executing a flawed decision. Teams adopting this pattern are reducing their false-positive incident rate by over 60% because the system itself acts as its own quality gate.

The second quiet revolution is the maturation of "cost-aware reasoning" in generative AI. The overlooked insight is not the ability to generate code or text, but the ability to estimate the compute cost of a response before generating it. Teams that implement cost budgets at the model-call level are discovering that their monthly inference spend drops by 30-40% simply because the system asks itself "is this query worth the compute?" before executing. This is not about throttling. It is about treating every prompt as a resource allocation decision.

The most under-discussed capability for hiring managers is the candidate who can explain why self-validation and cost-aware reasoning are not just operational niceties but architectural guarantees for preventing the most expensive AI failures: the undetected hallucination that reaches production and the unbounded inference cost that burns through a quarterly budget in a week. The engineer who understands that modern AI is about building systems that can audit themselves, not just generate outputs, will protect your organization from the trust and cost erosion that kills AI adoption.

For talent acquisition: the candidate who can articulate the difference between an AI that generates a response and an AI that can assess the quality of its own response before delivering it is the one who will build systems that are trusted in production. The candidate who can explain why every AI action must have a confidence threshold, a cost budget, and a human escalation path is the one who will design systems that are both autonomous and auditable.
